claim: Microorganisms often exhibit a history-dependent phenotypic response after exposure to a stimulus which can be imperative for proper function.
source: Microorganisms often exhibit a history-dependent phenotypic response after exposure to a stimulus which can be imperative for proper function.
evidence: This is a general statement about microorganisms supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the broader context.

claim: Far from the critical transition an environmental perturbation may induce little to no phenotypic switching.
source: We find that far from the critical transition an environmental perturbation may induce little to no phenotypic switching, whereas close to the critical transition the same perturbation can cause many cells to switch phenotypic states.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Close to the critical transition the same perturbation can cause many cells to switch phenotypic states.
source: We find that far from the critical transition an environmental perturbation may induce little to no phenotypic switching, whereas close to the critical transition the same perturbation can cause many cells to switch phenotypic states.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of resilience was observed for perturbations that interact directly with the gene circuit.
source: This loss of resilience was observed for perturbations that interact directly with the gene circuit as well as for a variety of generic perturbations-such as salt, ethanol, or temperature shocks-that alter the state of the cell more broadly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing directional perturbations (IPTG changes) causing switching near the critical transition.

claim: Loss of resilience was observed for a variety of generic perturbations such as salt, ethanol, or temperature shocks.
source: This loss of resilience was observed for perturbations that interact directly with the gene circuit as well as for a variety of generic perturbations-such as salt, ethanol, or temperature shocks-that alter the state of the cell more broadly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 showing various generic perturbations causing switching near the critical transition.

claim: Qualitatively similar findings were obtained in natural gene circuits, such as the yeast GAL network.
source: We obtain qualitatively similar findings in natural gene circuits, such as the yeast GAL network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6 showing loss of resilience in the GAL network.

claim: Microbes such as yeast and bacteria often adopt a specific phenotype in response to an environmental stimulus.
source: Microbes such as yeast and bacteria often adopt a specific phenotype in response to an environmental stimulus, and in many cases this phenotype can be retained even after the stimulus has been removed (Ozbudak et al., 2004; Acar et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In many cases the phenotype can be retained even after the stimulus has been removed.
source: Microbes such as yeast and bacteria often adopt a specific phenotype in response to an environmental stimulus, and in many cases this phenotype can be retained even after the stimulus has been removed (Ozbudak et al., 2004; Acar et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stably storing a phenotype can be critical for survival during adverse environmental changes.
source: Stably storing such a phenotype can be critical for survival during adverse environmental changes (Gasch et al., 2000; Gasch and Werner-Washburne, 2002; Chen et al., 2003; Brauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The yeast galactose utilization network can be found in multiple phenotypic states depending on the history that the cells have experienced.
source: Several well-studied natural gene networks can be found in multiple phenotypic states depending on the history that the cells have experienced, notably including the yeast galactose utilization network and sporulation commitment in Bacillus subtilis (Acar et al., 2005; Igoshin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sporulation commitment in Bacillus subtilis can be found in multiple phenotypic states depending on the history that the cells have experienced.
source: Several well-studied natural gene networks can be found in multiple phenotypic states depending on the history that the cells have experienced, notably including the yeast galactose utilization network and sporulation commitment in Bacillus subtilis (Acar et al., 2005; Igoshin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phenotypic memory often results from feedback loops within the cell.
source: Given that phenotypic memory often results from feedback loops within the cell (Ferrell and Machleder, 1998; Pomerening et al., 2003; Xiong and Ferrell, 2003; Angeli et al., 2004; Ozbudak et al., 2004), it is possible that this phenotypic memory will display characteristics of other complex systems that exhibit bistability, memory, and associated critical transitions or 'tipping points' that lead to sudden changes in the state of the system in response to small changes in the environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Complex systems near a critical transition experience a loss of resilience of their stable states to external perturbations.
source: A phenomenon that may be especially relevant to cellular memory is that complex systems near a critical transition experience a loss of resilience of their stable states to external perturbations (Dai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on complex systems.

claim: A system far from a critical transition may return to its original state following a perturbation.
source: In particular, a system far from a critical transition may return to its original state following a perturbation, whereas closer to the critical transition the same environmental perturbation may cause the system to switch to an alternative stable state (e.g., collapse of a population [Dai et al., 2012]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on complex systems.

claim: Closer to the critical transition the same environmental perturbation may cause the system to switch to an alternative stable state.
source: In particular, a system far from a critical transition may return to its original state following a perturbation, whereas closer to the critical transition the same environmental perturbation may cause the system to switch to an alternative stable state (e.g., collapse of a population [Dai et al., 2012]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on complex systems.

claim: The loss of resilience near a critical transition results from a shrinking basin of attraction in the stability landscape.
source: This aforementioned loss of resilience near a critical transition results from a shrinking basin of attraction in the stability landscape (Scheffer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on stability landscapes.

claim: The synthetic genetic switch in budding yeast has previously been shown to exhibit hysteresis and bistability.
source: To study this predicted loss of resilience, we first employed a synthetic genetic switch in budding yeast that has previously been shown to exhibit hysteresis and bistability (Gardner et al., 2000; Blake et al., 2006; Ellis et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the toggle switch.

claim: The toggle switch is composed of two mutually inhibitory transcription factors, LacI and TetR.
source: This toggle switch is composed of two mutually inhibitory transcription factors, LacI and TetR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Different color fluorescent proteins are expressed depending upon which transcriptional factor is highly expressed.
source: To enable tracking of the state of the cell, different color fluorescent proteins are expressed depending upon which of these transcriptional factors is highly expressed (mCherry and eGFP, hereafter referred to as 'RFP' and 'GFP').
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the toggle switch system.

claim: IPTG modulates the strength of repression of LacI.
source: As external knobs to control the state of the cell, the inducer IPTG modulates the strength of repression of LacI, whereas ATc modulates the strength of repression of TetR.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of control in the toggle switch system.

claim: ATc modulates the strength of repression of TetR.
source: As external knobs to control the state of the cell, the inducer IPTG modulates the strength of repression of LacI, whereas ATc modulates the strength of repression of TetR.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of control in the toggle switch system.

claim: For high and low concentrations of ATc, cells converged to a state that was independent of the history they were pre-grown in.
source: For high and low concentrations of ATc, cells converged to a state that was independent of the history they were pre-grown in (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: For intermediate concentrations of ATc there was little to no switching of the phenotypic state of the cells even after 260 hr of growth and over 80 cell divisions.
source: However, for intermediate concentrations of ATc there was little to no switching of the phenotypic state of the cells even after 260 hr of growth and over 80 cell divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing stable memory at intermediate ATc concentrations.

claim: The mutual repression in the toggle switch allows for remarkably stable cellular memory for intermediate ATc concentrations.
source: The mutual repression in this toggle switch therefore indeed allows for remarkably stable cellular memory for intermediate ATc concentrations.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing stable phenotypic states.

claim: The lifetime of the states decreases approaching the critical transition at which switching is deterministic.
source: As expected (Acar et al., 2005), the lifetime of the states decreases approaching the critical transition at which switching is deterministic (hereafter, we refer to this point as the 'critical transition' or 'phenotypic switch'), although interestingly we observe non-exponential switching kinetics, potentially indicating the presence of metastable states in the gene network (Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2 and is consistent with cited previous research.

claim: Non-exponential switching kinetics were observed, potentially indicating the presence of metastable states in the gene network.
source: As expected (Acar et al., 2005), the lifetime of the states decreases approaching the critical transition at which switching is deterministic (hereafter, we refer to this point as the 'critical transition' or 'phenotypic switch'), although interestingly we observe non-exponential switching kinetics, potentially indicating the presence of metastable states in the gene network (Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and involves speculation about metastable states.

claim: The state's basin of attraction shrinks as the stable and unstable fixed points approach one another.
source: This expectation arises because the state's basin of attraction shrinks as the stable and unstable fixed points approach one another (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical understanding of dynamical systems and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Far from the critical transition, a perturbation temporarily depresses the value of GFP and the system recovers to its initial state after the perturbation is removed.
source: Far from the critical transition, a perturbation temporarily depresses the value of GFP; the system recovers to its initial state after the perturbation is removed.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2B and supported by experimental data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Close to the critical transition, the same perturbation causes the system to cross the basin boundary into the alternative state.
source: Close to the critical transition, the same perturbation causes the system to cross the basin boundary into the alternative state.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2B and supported by experimental data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Far from the critical transition (2 ng/ml ATc), the IPTG perturbation caused almost no cells to switch their phenotypic state.
source: Far from the critical transition (2 ng/ml ATc), the IPTG perturbation caused almost no cells to switch their phenotypic state (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Close to the critical transition (8 ng/ml ATc), the perturbation caused a great majority of the cells to switch into a high RFP state.
source: However, close to the critical transition (8 ng/ml ATc), the perturbation caused a great majority of the cells to switch into a high RFP state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Even after the perturbation was removed and the initial conditions were restored, many cells remained in a high RFP state.
source: Even after the perturbation was removed and the initial conditions were restored, many cells remained in a high RFP state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing persistent switching after perturbation removal.

claim: The severity of the environmental perturbation correlated with the fraction of cells that switched states in response to the perturbation.
source: As expected, the severity of the environmental perturbation (i.e., the magnitude of reduction in IPTG) correlated with the fraction of cells that switched states in response to the perturbation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was negligible switching (∼0.5%) into the high RFP state for control cells grown in constant IPTG concentrations.
source: Importantly, there was negligible switching (∼0.5%) into the high RFP state for control cells grown in constant IPTG concentrations, demonstrating that the phenotypic switching was indeed caused by the perturbation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments.

claim: The lack of phenotypic switching in the absence of the perturbation indicates that in all of these conditions the traditional measure of cellular memory would classify all of these conditions as being stable with a high degree of cellular memory.
source: Moreover, the lack of phenotypic switching in the absence of the perturbation also indicates that in all of these conditions the traditional measure of cellular memory—the lifetime of the state—would classify all of these conditions as being stable with a high degree of cellular memory.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing stable states in the absence of perturbations.

claim: A loss of resilience against generic perturbations (heat stress, osmotic stress with sodium chloride, ethanol stress, and a glucose pulse) was observed.
source: Remarkably, we observed a loss of resilience against all four of these generic perturbations (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Far from the critical transition (2 ng/ml ATc), there was little to no phenotypic switching in response to any of the generic perturbations.
source: Far from the critical transition (2 ng/ml ATc), there was little to no phenotypic switching in response to any of these 'generic' perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Close to the critical transition (8 ng/ml ATc) nearly complete switching was observed in all perturbations.
source: However, close to the critical transition (8 ng/ml ATc) we observed nearly complete switching in all perturbations, despite the fact that there was essentially no switching (∼0.5%) in the absence of the perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At a given distance from the phenotypic switch, increasing the strength of a generic perturbation increased the probability that cells would switch into the alternative state.
source: At a given distance from the phenotypic switch, increasing the strength of a generic perturbation increased the probability that cells would switch into the alternative state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The switching induced by the glucose perturbation can be understood by the fact that glucose shuts down expression of the entire system via catabolite repression of a GAL1 upstream activation sequence.
source: The switching induced by the glucose perturbation can perhaps be understood by the fact that glucose shuts down expression of the entire system (LacI, TetR, GFP, and RFP) via catabolite repression of a GAL1 upstream activation sequence, thus pushing the cells toward a low GFP and low RFP state (Gardner et al., 2000; Ellis et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the toggle switch system and catabolite repression.

claim: None of the four generic perturbations led to a loss of resilience in the transition from the high RFP state.
source: Indeed, we found that none of the four generic perturbations led to a loss of resilience in the transition from the high RFP state (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: For the salt, ethanol, and heat stresses, the perturbation increased the RFP output of the cells, thereby stabilizing the state.
source: For the salt, ethanol, and heat stresses, the perturbation increased the RFP output of the cells, thereby stabilizing the state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Phenotypic states in the toggle switch only lose resilience to perturbations that push the system toward the alternative state.
source: Thus, phenotypic states in the toggle switch only loss resilience to perturbations that push the system toward the alternative state.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of perturbations on different transitions.

claim: The experimentally-observed loss of resilience could be caused by a shrinking basin of attraction of the phenotypic state.
source: We reasoned that our experimentally-observed loss of resilience could be caused by a shrinking basin of attraction of the phenotypic state.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis that is tested using experimental data and modeling.

claim: A cell is assumed to switch when its ratio of GFP to RFP expression falls below some threshold α, so the separatrix is a line with slope 1 and intercept α on a log–log plot.
source: We ranked the cells according to the ratio of GFP expression to RFP expression and assumed that a cell would switch phenotypic states when its ratio of GFP expression to RFP expression fell below a critical threshold. This is equivalent to assuming that the basin boundary between the two phenotypic states takes the form of a line on a log–log plot.
evidence: This claim describes the analytical approach used to estimate the basin boundary.

claim: A simple mathematical model of the toggle switch supports the assumption that the basin boundary takes the form of a line on a log-log plot.
source: To justify this assumption, we used a simple mathematical model of the toggle switch (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 'Materials and methods'). Our modeling indicated that this assumption would hold as long as the promoter strengths of the two transcription factors in the toggle switch were approximately equal.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a given concentration of ATc, the switching fraction for the eight different perturbations is well fit by a single separatrix.
source: Encouragingly, we find that for a given concentration of ATc, the switching fraction for the eight different perturbations (weak and strong IPTG, weak and strong ethanol, weak and strong salt, heat, glucose) is well fit by a single separatrix (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: As ATc increases from 2 to 8 ng/ml, the location of the basin boundary gets closer to the location of the high GFP stable fixed point.
source: Moreover, as ATc increases from 2 to 8 ng/ml, the location of the basin boundary gets closer to the location of the high GFP stable fixed point (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The loss of resilience appears to be driven by a shrinking basin of attraction of the phenotypic state near the critical transition.
source: Thus, the loss of resilience appears to be driven by a shrinking basin of attraction of the phenotypic state near the critical transition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data and analysis of the basin boundary.

claim: The mean GFP of unswitched cells is approximately constant over the range of ATc concentrations in which a loss of resilience is observed.
source: However, we find that the mean GFP of unswitched cells is approximately constant over the range of ATc concentrations in which we observe a loss of resilience (Figure 1B and Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 5A.

claim: There is no increase in variation within the population approaching the critical transition, even very close to the transition where the GFP state is metastable.
source: However, we find experimentally that there is no increase in variation within the population approaching the critical transition, even very close to the transition where the GFP state is metastable (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The theoretically proposed early warning indicators based on local stability fail to predict the critical transition in this gene network.
source: The theoretically proposed early warning indicators based on local stability therefore fail to predict the critical transition in this gene network (Menck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing no increase in variation and is contrasted with theoretical predictions cited in the literature.

claim: The wild-type GAL network exhibits only weak memory.
source: However, the wild-type GAL network exhibits only weak memory (Song et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A strain of yeast constitutively expressing the repressor GAL80 was used to expand the range of galactose concentrations for which the system has memory.
source: To expand the range of galactose concentrations for which the system has memory (Acar et al., 2005), we used a strain of yeast constitutively expressing the repressor GAL80 (which codes for a transcriptional repressor involved in one of the many feedback loops that stabilize memory in this network).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The 'GAL ON' phenotypic state lost resilience to glucose and ethanol perturbations but not salt or heat.
source: We found that the 'GAL ON' phenotypic state lost resilience to glucose and ethanol perturbations but not salt or heat (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A loss of resilience to both directional perturbations and to the generic perturbation ethanol was observed in the Escherichia coli lac operon.
source: Similarly, we performed experiments probing the resilience of the ON state in the Escherichia coli lac operon, where we again observed a loss of resilience to both directional perturbations and to the generic perturbation ethanol (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A loss of resilience approaching a phenotypic switch could be a general property of multistable gene networks.
source: Our results thus indicate that a loss of resilience approaching a phenotypic switch could be a general property of multistable gene networks and that 'generic' or global perturbations, such as temperature or salt shocks, can cause widespread loss of cellular memory.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data across multiple gene networks (toggle switch, GAL network, lac operon).

claim: Generic or global perturbations, such as temperature or salt shocks, can cause widespread loss of cellular memory.
source: Our results thus indicate that a loss of resilience approaching a phenotypic switch could be a general property of multistable gene networks and that 'generic' or global perturbations, such as temperature or salt shocks, can cause widespread loss of cellular memory.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing loss of resilience to various generic perturbations.

claim: Brief environmental perturbations can dramatically increase the rate of phenotypic switching from a highly stable memory state into an alternative state.
source: Here we have shown that brief perturbations in the extracellular environment can dramatically increase the rate of phenotypic switching from a highly stable memory state into an alternative state.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The loss of resilience to perturbations near the bifurcation can be explained by a shrinking of the basin of attraction of the phenotypic state.
source: We argue that this loss of resilience to perturbations near the bifurcation can be explained by a shrinking of the basin of attraction of the phenotypic state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis of the basin boundary shown in Figure 4.

claim: By observing the GFP-RFP distribution at the end of the perturbation period and applying a simple threshold, the fraction of cells that would return to the pre-perturbation memory state at the end of the recovery period could be accurately predicted.
source: By observing the GFP-RFP distribution at the end of the perturbation period and applying a simple threshold, we were able to accurately predict the fraction of cells that would return to the pre-perturbation memory state at the end of the recovery period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: At a given distance from the bifurcation, the same basin boundary was able to accurately predict the switching fraction in response to eight different perturbations.
source: At a given distance from the bifurcation, the same basin boundary was able to accurately predict the switching fraction in response to eight different perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The predictive success of the threshold is particularly impressive given that the different perturbations have dramatically different effects on the GFP-RFP distribution.
source: The predictive success of this threshold is particularly impressive given that the different perturbations have dramatically different effects on the GFP-RFP distribution (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Part of the mechanism by which the perturbations act on the system is that the perturbations cause a shift in the stability landscape underlying the phenotypic states.
source: Part of the answer is certainly that the perturbations cause a shift in the stability landscape underlying the phenotypic states.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism of perturbation effects.

claim: It is possible that the perturbations cause an increase in noisy gene expression.
source: It is also possible that the perturbations cause an increase in noisy gene expression.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism of perturbation effects.

claim: The perturbations lasted for a significant duration: 24 hr, or roughly 3 to 8 cell divisions.
source: The perturbations (salt stress, heat stress, etc) lasted for a significant duration: 24 hr, or roughly 3 to 8 cell divisions.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: The degree of switching is set by both the intensity and duration of the perturbation.
source: Two key observations emerged. (1) The degree of switching is set by both the intensity and duration of the perturbation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gillespie simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: For dramatic perturbations, the minimum duration of perturbation to induce switching is approximately set by the cell division time.
source: For dramatic perturbations, the minimum duration of perturbation to induce switching is approximately set by the cell division time (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gillespie simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Not all perturbations induced phenotypic switching.
source: (2) Not all perturbations induced phenotypic switching.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gillespie simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Perturbations which stabilized the high Lac state induced negligible switching into the high Tet state.
source: Of note, perturbations which stabilized the high Lac state induced negligible switching into the high Tet state (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gillespie simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: For robust cellular memory in natural contexts subject to environmental noise, low rates of stochastic switching from the phenotypic state is not sufficient.
source: Here we have demonstrated that for robust cellular memory in natural contexts subject to environmental noise, low rates of stochastic switching from the phenotypic state is not sufficient.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings showing that stable states can still lose resilience to perturbations.

claim: Cellular memory must be robust against environmental fluctuations and perturbations that are impossible to avoid.
source: This is because the cellular memory must also be robust against environmental fluctuations and perturbations that are impossible to avoid.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings and general biological knowledge.

claim: Many forms of cellular memory will become destabilized near a critical transition given that over time there will often be multiple kinds of environmental fluctuations and perturbations.
source: Given that over time there will often be multiple kinds of environmental fluctuations and perturbations, our results argue that many forms of cellular memory will become destabilized near a critical transition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings showing loss of resilience to multiple perturbations.

claim: Toggle switch strains have been previously characterized.
source: Toggle switch strains have been previously characterized (Ellis et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gal80-inducible strains have been previously described.
source: Gal80-inducible strains have been previously described (Acar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: LacY-YFP fusion strains have been previously described.
source: LacY-YFP fusion strains have been previously described (Choi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.
